summary: Describes what network elements must do to deliver Guaranteed service, which gives applications firm limits on delay and a reserved amount of bandwidth. It is for applications that need predictable timing.

eli5.summary: It is a promise that your data will arrive within a set time and with enough room, like a reserved delivery truck with a promised arrival time.

questions: what is guaranteed service in intserv
how is end to end queueing delay bounded
what are the c and d error terms
what is a tspec and rspec
subtitle: What a router must do to give a flow a provable cap on queueing delay and no queue-overflow loss.

tldr.problem: Some applications, such as audio and video play-back, cannot tolerate any datagram arriving after its deadline, but ordinary best-effort delivery makes no timing promise.
tldr.mechanism: A flow is described by a token bucket, and each network element approximates a dedicated wire of rate R and reports two error terms, C and D. Adding those terms along the path gives a mathematically provable bound on end-to-end queueing delay.
tldr.outcome: A policed flow that stays within its traffic description gets an assured bandwidth, a bounded queueing delay and no queueing loss. The service needs every element on the path to support it, and it is subject to admission control.

today: RFC 2212 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text itself says the setup mechanism is outside its scope and points to RFC 2210 for use with RSVP.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 2212 defines the requirements for network elements that support guaranteed service. It is one of a series of documents that specify the network element behavior needed to support various qualities of service in IP internetworks, and it follows the service specification template of RFC 2216.

The idea in brief: a flow is described using a token bucket. Given that description, each service element (a router, a subnet and so on) computes parameters describing how it will handle the flow's data. Combining the parameters from every element on a path gives the maximum delay a piece of data will experience.

The RFC stresses three points. First, the setup mechanism is not specified: a guaranteed reservation could be made with a protocol like RSVP, by manual configuration of routers, or with a network management protocol like SNMP. Second, every element on the path must support guaranteed service or adequately mimic it, but partial deployment is still useful, for example inside an intranet or in an ISP backbone. Third, applications keep considerable control over their delay, because queueing delay depends mainly on the bucket size b and the requested rate R.
sections.eli5: The rules say how every stop on a delivery route must behave so the total waiting time can be added up in advance. They do not say how you book the route, only what the route must promise.

sections.title: End-to-End Behavior and Motivation
sections.content:
The end-to-end behavior is an assured level of bandwidth that, when used by a policed flow, produces a delay-bounded service with no queueing loss for all conforming datagrams. This assumes no failure of network components and no routing change during the life of the flow.

Only the maximal queueing delay is controlled. The service does not control the minimal or average delay, and it does not try to minimize jitter. To get the full delay a datagram can see, the path latency must be determined and added to the guaranteed queueing delay. The RFC notes that a conservative bound on latency can be found by observing the delay of any one packet.

The service targets applications that need a firm guarantee that a datagram arrives no later than a certain time after it was sent. Because the bound is firm, it has to cover extremely rare long delays, so most datagrams arrive far earlier and must be buffered at the receiver until play-back time. The RFC calls this one extreme end of delay control, and it is typically useful only if every router and link along the path provides it.
sections.eli5: The promise is only about the longest you might wait in line, not the average. Most of the time your parcel will arrive early and will just sit until it is needed.

sections.title: Data Handling Requirements
sections.content:
A network element MUST make its service approximate the fluid model: the service a dedicated wire of bandwidth R between source and receiver would give. In that model a flow's service is independent of every other flow. At each element the flow's level of service is characterized by a service rate R and a buffer size B.

The fluid delay of a flow obeying a token bucket (r,b) and served at rate R is bounded by b/R as long as R is no less than r. Real elements deviate a little, so the element MUST ensure that the queueing delay of any datagram is less than b/R+C/R+D, where C and D describe the maximal local deviation from the fluid model.

Giving better service than this is allowed. A flow that is not using its share can have the spare bandwidth lent to others, and algorithms such as Weighted Fair Queueing that do this are encouraged. Links must not fragment datagrams as part of guaranteed service, and datagrams larger than the link MTU are policed as nonconformant.
sections.eli5: Pretend each flow has its own private pipe. Real routers share pipes, but they must behave nearly the same as if the pipe were private, with only a small, known amount of slop.

sections.title: Describing Traffic and Requesting Service
sections.content:
Guaranteed service is invoked by giving the network element a TSpec (the traffic) and an RSpec (the desired service). A request with a new TSpec or RSpec is treated as a new invocation, so admission control SHOULD be applied again, but a flow that only reduces its TSpec or RSpec SHOULD never be denied service.

The TSpec is a token bucket plus extra limits: bucket rate r and bucket depth b (both positive), peak rate p (at least r, or infinity if unknown), minimum policed unit m and maximum datagram size M. Rates are in bytes of IP datagrams per second, from 1 byte per second up to 40 terabytes per second. The depth ranges from 1 byte to 250 gigabytes. Datagrams smaller than m are counted as size m, and a flow MUST be rejected if M is larger than the link MTU.

The RSpec is a rate R, which MUST be at least r, and a slack term S in microseconds, which MUST be nonnegative. A higher R lowers queueing delay. Slack is the gap between the delay the application wants and the delay it would get at rate R, and an element may use it to reserve fewer resources. No buffer size is in the RSpec: the element derives the buffer it needs.

The TSpec can be sent as three single-precision IEEE floating point numbers (r, b, p) followed by two 32-bit integers in network byte order (m, M). The slack term is a 32-bit integer from 0 to (232)-1 microseconds.
sections.eli5: You tell the network how big a bucket of data you may dump at once and how fast you usually send. Then you pick how fast a lane you want, and you can say how much extra waiting time you would still be happy with.

sections.title: Error Terms C and D and the Delay Bound
sections.content:
Each element exports two error terms that say how far it deviates from the fluid model, and both add up along a path. C is the rate-dependent term, measured in bytes. Its effect is divided by the reservation rate R, as with the time taken to serialize a datagram split into ATM cells. D is the rate-independent, per-element term, measured in microseconds. It is the worst-case non-rate-based transit time variation through the element and is generally set at boot or configuration time.

An element can advertise C from 1 to 228 and D from 1 to 228, and the totals along a path are capped at (232)-1. The path sums are called Ctot and Dtot. The partial sums from the most recent reshaping point are Csum and Dsum, and they let each element work out the buffering it needs.

With these, an end node can compute the worst-case queueing delay. The RFC's example is an application intolerant of any lost or late datagram: it computes the bound from Ctot, Dtot and its TSpec, and sets its play-back point to that value. Without a known peak rate, the delay simplifies to b/R+Ctot/R+Dtot.

The mechanisms that collect the per-hop terms and tell the applications are outside this document. They come from reservation setup protocols, routing protocols or other management functions.
sections.eli5: Every stop on the route says how much extra delay it might add, some depending on your lane speed and some not. Add up all the stops and you know the worst-case trip time.

sections.title: Policing and Reshaping
sections.content:
Two kinds of enforcement exist. Policing compares arriving traffic with the TSpec and is done only at the edge of the network. Reshaping delays datagrams until they fit the TSpec again, and it is done at heterogeneous source branch points and at source merge points. Inside the network, an element that wants to police MUST reshape instead, because queueing can make traffic that entered conformant look nonconformant downstream.

Traffic must obey the rule that over any time period T the data sent cannot exceed M+min[pT, rT+b-M]. Nonconforming datagrams SHOULD be treated as best effort and, if marking becomes available, marked as noncompliant. The RFC explains why dropping them is risky: a receiver with an inadequate TSpec could pre-empt a best-effort receiver and cut off its traffic. The action for nonconforming datagrams SHOULD be configurable.

A reshaper must start with a full token bucket and needs buffering of b+Csum+(Dsum*r) to restore conforming traffic to its original shape. If the buffer is full when a datagram arrives, that datagram is nonconforming. Given an accurate TSpec, reshaping adds little actual delay and does not affect the delay bound.
sections.eli5: At the door, a guard checks you are not carrying more than you promised. Later in the building, nobody tells you off for being bunched up. They just hold you briefly and let you out in a neat line.

sections.title: Ordering, Merging and Implementation Guidelines
sections.content:
The RFC defines how TSpecs are ordered and combined. TSpec A is a substitute for TSpec B if it is at least as large in r, b, p and M and at least as small in m. A merged TSpec takes the largest rate, bucket and peak rate and the smallest minimum policed unit and maximum datagram size. RSpecs merge by taking the largest R and the smallest S. A node that uses slack must keep the delay constraint Sout + b/Rout + Ctoti/Rout no larger than Sin + b/Rin + Ctoti/Rin, with r no larger than Rout and Rout no larger than Rin. It also stores the slack it used and applies the same value on reservation refreshes.

Implementors are told that subnetworks are network elements too, so routers act as proxies for them. Link-level headers and tunnel headers add to the IP rate, so subnetworks MUST adjust the rate and possibly the bucket size. For weighted fair queueing, D is set to the link MTU divided by the link bandwidth and C to M. For a slotted system such as Stop and Go queueing, D is the maximum number of slots a datagram may wait.

Elements must ensure delay bounds are never violated and datagrams are not lost for conforming sources, and that misbehaving flows do not affect others. The RFC names Weighted Fair Queueing, Jitter-EDD and Virtual Clock as algorithms that approximate the fluid model. It also admits an open problem: shared RSVP reservations are hard to handle where several sources meet, because the RSpec rate is tied to a particular delay bound.
sections.eli5: There are rules for combining several bookings into one and for making sure no stop on the route cheats. Builders are warned that wrappers, like extra headers, take up room too.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security section is brief. It says the memo discusses how this service could be abused to permit denial of service attacks, and that the service as defined does not allow denial of service, although service may degrade under certain circumstances.

The discussion it points to is the policing text: if nonconforming datagrams were simply discarded, a receiver asking for a reservation with an inadequate TSpec and RSpec could stop a best-effort receiver from getting the flow. Treating nonconforming datagrams as best effort avoids that, though a bad TSpec may still increase queueing delays.
sections.eli5: The rules are written so a troublemaker cannot use a booking to block other people. The worst they can do is make things slower for themselves and a bit for their own flow.
